abstract: Amide-to-ester substitutions are used to study the role of the amide bonds of the protein backbone in protein structure, function, and folding. An amber suppressor tRNA/synthetase pair has been reported for incorporation of p-hydroxy-phenyl-L-lactic acid (HPLA), thereby introducing ester substitution at tyrosine residues. However, the application of this approach was limited due to the low yields of the modified proteins and the high cost of HPLA. Here we report the in vivo generation of HPLA from the significantly cheaper phenyl-L-lactic acid. We also construct an optimized plasmid with the HPLA suppressor tRNA/synthetase pair that provides higher yields of the modified proteins. The combination of the new plasmid and the in-situ generation of HPLA provides a facile and economical approach for introducing tyrosine ester substitutions. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by introducing tyrosine ester substitutions into the K + channel KcsA and the integral membrane enzyme GlpG. We introduce the tyrosine ester in the selectivity filter of the M96V mutant of the KcsA to probe the role of the second ion binding site in the conformation of the selectivity filter and the process of inactivation. We use tyrosine ester substitutions in GlpG to perturb backbone H-bonds to investigate the contribution of these H-bonds to membrane protein stability. We anticipate that the approach developed in this study will facilitate further investigations using tyrosine ester substitutions.
methods:
Experimental procedures
Construction of the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid
A pBK plasmid carrying the HPLA-RS gene (
21
) and the pULTRA plasmid used (pULTRA-CNF, Addgene plasmid # 48215) were gifts from Dr Peter Schultz. Prior to the transfer of the HPLA-RS gene, the spectinomycin resistance gene on the pULTRA plasmid (
26
) was replaced by the kanamycin resistance gene from pRSF1b (EMD Millipore). This change in antibiotic resistance was necessary for carrying out protein expression in TOP10 cells. We then substituted the NotI site at the 5′ end of the pCNF-RS gene on the pULTRA plasmid with a NdeI site. We PCR amplified the HPLA-RS gene from the pBK plasmid with a 5′ NdeI and a 3′ NotI site and used this PCR fragment to exchange the pCNF-RS with the HPLA-RS gene to provide the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid (
Fig. S1
) used in this study.
Super-folder Green Fluorescent Protein (sfGFP)
Expression
SfGFP in a pBAD vector (Fisher Scientific) with a TAG stop codon at N150 and a C-terminal His tag was provided by Dr Ryan Mehl (Oregon State University) (
23
). For protein expression,
E. coli
TOP10 cells (Fisher Scientific) were transformed with the sfGFP and the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmids. The transformants were cultured in LB media at 37 °C with ampicillin (0.1 mg/ml), kanamycin (0.05 mg/ml), and 1 mM PLA (Astatech) or HPLA (ChemImpex) to an
A
600
of 1.0. Protein expression was then induced by the addition of 1 mM IPTG (for the expression of the synthetase) and 0.1 % (w/v) of arabinose (for expression of sfGFP) and the cells were grown for 4 h at 37 °C. The cells were harvested by centrifugation, and resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Hepes, pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 1 mM MgCl
2
, 0.2 mg/ml lysozyme, 0.01 mg/ml DNAse, 1 mM PMSF) and lysed by sonication. The cell lysate was clarified by centrifugation and the sfGFP proteins were purified by Co
2+
affinity chromatography. The molecular weight of the sfGFP purified was determined by Electrospray Ionization Mass spectrometry (ESI-MS) and carried out by the Proteomics Core at OHSU.
Crystallization and structure determination.
For crystallization, the C-terminal His tag was removed by treatment with trypsin in a 1:50 ratio at 4 °C for 1 h. Following trypsinolysis, the GFP proteins were purified by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) in 20 mM Hepes, pH 7.5, and 100 mM NaCl. Following purification by SEC, the GFP proteins were concentrated to 17 mg/ml, and GFP crystals were grown in sitting drops by mixing 1 μl of the protein with 1 μl of a crystallization solution (50 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 25% PEG 4000). Crystals were cryoprotected by the addition of 20% glycerol and frozen in liquid Nitrogen. X-ray diffraction data were collected at the ALS 4.2.2 beamline and the data were integrated and scaled using XDS (
55
). The structure was solved by molecular replacement using Phaser (
56
) with the wild-type SfGFP structure (PDB ID:
5EHU
) as the search model, refined using automated refinement in Phenix and manual adjustments using COOT (
57
,
58
). X-ray data collection and refinement statistics are summarized in
Table S1
.
KcsA channel
Expression
We generated a TAG stop codon at Y78 in a KcsA construct with a C-terminal His tag in a pBAD vector. We also generated KcsA constructs with an M96V and with an M96V + Y78TAG substitutions. For protein expression, KcsA-pBAD plasmids were transformed into TOP10 cells along with the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid. The transformants were cultured in LB media at 37 °C with ampicillin (0.1 mg/ml), kanamycin (0.05 mg/ml), and 1 mM PLA to an
A
600
of 1.0. Protein expression was induced by the addition of 1 mM IPTG and 0.1 % (w/v) of arabinose and the cells were grown for 4 h at 37 °C. For Y78ester incorporation into the KcsA channel using the original approach, we cloned the KcsA construct with a Y78TAG substitution into a pBAD plasmid that also contained the
Methanocaldococcus jannaschii
amber suppressor tyrosyl-tRNA gene (
21
). For protein expression, this plasmid was transformed into TOP10 cells along with a pBK plasmid bearing the HPLA-RS gene (
21
), and protein expression was carried out as previously described (
18
). The cells were harvested by centrifugation, resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 250 mM Sucrose, 1 mM MgCl
2
) and membranes were prepared as previously described (
59
). The membranes were solubilized by 2% (w/v) decyl-β-D-maltoside (DM) and the KcsA proteins were purified by Co
2+
-affinity chromatography.
Crystallization and structure determination
Prior to crystallization, the C-terminal 35 residues of the KcsA channels were removed by treatment with chymotrypsin at 1:15 ratio (chymotrypsin: protein) for 2 h at room temperature (
29
). The chymotrypsinized channels were purified by SEC in 50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM KCl, 0.25% DM, pH 7.5 (SEC buffer). The KcsA channels were complexed with a Fab fragment from KcsA IgG (
10
). The KcsA -Fab complexes were purified by SEC with 10 mM Tetra butyl ammonium iodide (TBA) added to the SEC buffer. KcsA+TBA+Fab crystals were grown by mixing 1 μl of the protein with 1 μl of well solution [25–28% PEG 400 (v/v), 50 mM magnesium acetate, 50 mM MES pH 6.0–6.5]. KcsA crystals were cryo-protected by increasing the PEG 400 concentration in the reservoir to 42% (v/v) and were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. X-ray diffraction data were collected at the ALS 4.2.2 beamline and the diffraction data were integrated and scaled using XDS (
55
).
The structures were solved by molecular replacement using Phaser (
56
) with the wild-type structure (PDB:
1K4C
) as the search model. KcsA channel residues 74 to 79, lipids, water and ions were omitted from the search model. The residues deleted from the model prior to molecular replacement were manually built using Coot (
58
). The models were refined using automated refinement in Phenix (
57
) and manual refinement using COOT. X-ray data collection and refinement statistics are summarized in the
Table S1
.
GlpG
Expression
GlpG (residues 87–276) (
60
) was PCR amplified from
E. coli
genomic DNA and cloned in a pBAD vector with a C-terminal His tag. TAG stop codons were introduced at Y160, Y205, and Y224 by Quickchange mutagenesis. For protein expression, the pBAD-GlpG- TAG plasmids were transformed into TOP10 cells along with the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid. The transformants were cultured in LB media at 37 °C with 1 mM PLA. Protein expression and preparation of membranes were carried out as previously described for the KcsA channel. The membranes were solubilized by using 2% (w/v) DM and the GlpG proteins were purified by Co
2+
-affinity chromatography. The GlpG proteins were further purified by SEC in 50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM KCl, 0.25% DM, pH 7.5.
Equilibrium unfolding and refolding of GlpG
The equilibrium unfolding of wild-type and ester-incorporated GlpG was performed as described in Paslawski
et al.
, 2015 (
44
). Briefly, 0.5 μM of protein was added to 40 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.5 buffer containing 10 mM DDM, and varying concentrations of SDS to obtain SDS mole fractions (χ
SDS
) between 0 to 0.9 and incubated at 30 °C for 2 h. For refolding experiments, GlpG at 10 μM was initially unfolded in 10 mM SDS for 2 h at 25 °C, and then mixed with buffer containing various concentrations of SDS and DDM to the appropriate χ
SDS
values. Trp fluorescence emission spectra were recorded using 1 cm path length quartz cuvettes at 30 °C at 320 to 370 nm with an excitation at 280 nm. Excitation and emission slits with a nominal bandpass of 5 nm were used for all measurements. Three spectra were averaged for each measurement. Fluorescence emission maxima was obtained by parameterizing the emission spectra as described previously (

body:
Proteins are made of a linear chain of amino acids that are linked by amide bonds. Hydrogen bond formation by the amide bonds in the protein backbone drives the formation of the protein secondary structure. Incorporation of an α hydroxy-acid in place of an amino acid results in the generation of an ester linkage instead of an amide linkage. In the ester linkage, a hydrogen bond donor is replaced by a hydrogen bond acceptor (
1
). Amide-to-ester substitutions have been used to determine the energetic contribution of backbone hydrogen bonds in protein stability and folding (
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
,
6
,
7
). Amide-to-ester substitutions have also been used to study the contribution of backbone H-bonds to protein function and in the binding of ligands (
6
,
7
). In the field of ion channels, ester substitutions have been used to probe the role of structural changes in the transmembrane segments during channel function (
8
,
9
) The ester substitution reduces by roughly one-half the electronegativity at the carbonyl oxygen atom (
1
). In ion channels and transporters, the carbonyl oxygens are frequently used for constructing binding sites for ions and ligands (
10
,
11
). Ester substitutions have been used to probe the role of the ion-binding sites (
12
,
13
,
14
).
Ester incorporation into proteins has been carried out by amber suppression using an
in vitro
translation system with tRNAs chemically acylated with hydroxy-acids or alternately by using
Xenopus
oocyte expression (
2
,
8
,
9
,
15
). The amount of protein obtained in these systems is quite low and is mainly suitable for functional studies of the mutant proteins. Alternately, ester substitutions have been introduced by chemical synthesis using total or semisynthetic approaches (
5
,
12
,
16
,
17
,
18
). However, these synthetic approaches are limited to small and medium-sized proteins and require the ability to carry out
in vitro
folding of the protein.
The development of orthogonal tRNA synthetases in conjunction with cognate nonsense suppressor tRNAs has revolutionized the incorporation of unnatural modifications into proteins (
19
,
20
). The Schultz lab has previously described a synthetase/tRNA pair for the incorporation of p-hydroxy-phenyl L-lactic (HPLA) acid at introduced amber stop codons thereby introducing an ester linkage into the protein (
21
). Substitutions at the Tyr residue result in replacing the Tyr amide linkage with an ester linkage (
Fig. 1
A
). Use of this system however only afforded low yields of the ester-containing protein and another limitation was the cost of the hydroxy acid necessary. These limitations made it quite challenging to use this system for incorporation of Tyr ester substitutions, particularly for ester incorporation into membrane proteins, which are generally expressed at lower levels.
Figure 1
Amide to ester substitution in the protein backbone.
A
, using the nonsense suppression approach for amide to ester incorporation in the protein backbone. The HPLA-synthetase loads the cognate suppressor tRNA with the hydroxy acid which is incorporated during suppression of the amber stop codon to generate an ester linkage instead of an amide bond.
B
, structures of amino acids and α-hydroxy acids. HPLA, hydroxy-phenyl lactic acid and PLA, phenyl lactic acid.
C
, suppression of the 150TAG codon in sfGFP. Fluorescence and SDS-PAGE of sfGFP purified from the cultures under the various growth conditions is indicated. Suppression of the 150TAG codon in sfGFP is only observed when the HPLA-RS plasmid that carries both the synthetase and the suppressor tRNA is present along with PLA or HPLA added to the growth medium. Some cleavage of the ester containing sfGFP takes place due to high pH encountered during SDS-PAGE.
Here we develop a facile approach for efficient and economical incorporation of Tyr esters into proteins. We use the facile approach to incorporate Tyr ester substitutions into the K
+
channel KcsA and the rhomboid protease GlpG. We use the Tyr ester substitution in the KcsA channel to probe the role of a specific ion binding site. We use Tyr ester substitutions in the GlpG protein to probe the contribution of the main chain H-bonds to the stability of an integral membrane protein.
Results
Conversion of phenyl-lactic acid to hydroxyphenyl lactic acid in
E. coli
The
t-
RNA synthetases selected for the incorporation of the unnatural amino acids strongly discriminate between the unnatural amino acid and the naturally occurring amino acids but do not show a high level of discrimination between closely related unnatural amino acids (
22
,
23
,
24
,
25
). For example, the PheCN synthetase can incorporate a variety of Tyr and Phe derivative unnatural amino acids (
24
). The HPLA synthetase (HPLA-RS) incorporates HPLA in response to an amber codon and provides a means for introducing an amide to ester substitution at Tyr residues (
Fig. 1
A
) (
21
). We tested whether the HPLA-RS is similarly permissive or poly-specific and can incorporate the closely related phenyl -L- lactic acid (PLA) as a potential approach for introducing amide to ester substitutions at Phe residues (
Fig. 1
B
).
Prior to our tests, we transferred the HPLA-RS to a pULTRA plasmid (
26
). In the pULTRA plasmid, the expression of the synthetase is driven by the
tacI
promoter while the expression of the cognate amber suppressor tRNA is driven by a
proK
promoter (
Fig. S1
). The use of the pULTRA plasmid has previously been shown to improve suppression efficiency (
26
). We are mainly interested in membrane proteins and we routinely express membrane proteins using a pBAD expression vector and TOP10 cells. To facilitate the use of the HPLA-RS plasmid in TOP10 cells, we generated a variant of the pULTRA plasmid that carries a kanamycin resistance gene.
For measurements of amber suppression, we used a super folder Green Fluorescent Protein (sfGFP) gene with an amber stop codon at N150 as the reporter (
23
). For our expression tests, the sfGFP 150TAG plasmid was co-transformed with the HPLA-RS plasmid into TOP10 cells. We observed robust GFP expression when HPLA was added to the medium (
Fig. 1
C
). Surprisingly, we also observed robust GFP expression when PLA was added to the medium. We observed no GFP expression when PLA or HPLA were not added or in the absence of the HPLA-RS plasmid.
We purified the full-length GFP obtained by suppression using HPLA or PLA and used base hydrolysis to check for the presence of the ester linkage (
27
). We observed base cleavage of the GFP polypeptide indicating the presence of the ester linkage due to the incorporation of the hydroxy acid (
Fig. 2
A
). Next, we determined the mass of the GFP protein obtained with PLA added to the growth media to confirm the incorporation of PLA. We observed that the mass measured with PLA added to the medium was 16 Da. greater than the mass calculated for GFP with PLA (
Fig. 2
B
). The mass difference corresponded to the addition of a hydroxy group and was similar to the mass observed for GFP purified from cells with HPLA added to the growth media (
Fig. S2
). These experiments therefore suggested the incorporation of HPLA into sfGFP at the 150TAG even though PLA was added to the growth medium.
Figure 2

A

SDS/PAGE gel showing that treatment with NaOH has no effect on the WT sfGFP whereas similar treatment of the sfGFP 150TAG purified from cells grown in PLA results in cleavage of the polypeptide (− indicates before hydrolysis while + indicates after hydrolysis).
B

The charge spectrum is shown and the inset corresponds to the reconstructed mass spectra. The lower mass observed (27,747.1 Da.) corresponds to the deletion of the N-terminal Met.
C
, crystal structure of sfGFP 150TAG obtained with PLA added to the media. A superposition of the sfGFP 150TAG purified from cells grown with PLA overlaid with the WT sfGFP is shown in cartoon representation. Residue 150, the site of the unnatural incorporation is indicated by a red sphere.

To probe the side chain incorporated, we purified GFP obtained by expression with PLA added. We crystallized the protein and solved the structure (
Fig. 2
C
,
Table S1
). We observed clear density for the presence of a 4′ hydroxy group on the benzyl side chain (
Fig. 2
,
D
and
E
) confirming the incorporation of HPLA at position 150. These results suggest that the PLA added to the growth media is converted into HPLA and then subsequently incorporated into sfGFP.
We were unable to find a literature precedent for the conversion of PLA to HPLA by
Escherichia coli.
Conversion of Phe to Tyr by hydroxylation does not take place in
E. coli
as it lacks the Phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme that is present in higher organisms (
28
). While the pathway for conversion of PLA to HPLA in
E. coli
is presently not known, it is of practical benefit as PLA is roughly 100-fold less expensive than HPLA, which substantially reduces the cost for Tyr ester incorporation. The
in vivo
generation of HPLA combined with the use of the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid gave improved yields and provided an efficient means for incorporating Tyr ester substitutions. We also tested BL21 (DE3) cells and similarly observed ester incorporation into sfGFP-150TAG by using the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid and PLA in the growth media (
Fig. S3
).
Tyr ester incorporation in the selectivity filter of the K
+
channel KcsA
Next, we tested our optimized protocol for an ester substitution at Tyr78 in the selectivity filter of the KcsA K
+
channel. The selectivity filter refers to the ion-binding sites in a K
+
channel and is formed from a highly conserved amino acid sequence of TVGYG (residues 75–79 in the KcsA channel,
Fig. 3
A
) (
29
,
30
). The selectivity filter consists of four K
+
binding sites (called S1 to S4, extracellular to intracellular) that are built using the main chain carbonyl oxygens of the conserved sequence and the hydroxyl side chain of Thr. K
+
ions bind sequentially to these sites during transit through the channel. This conformation of the selectivity filter is referred to as “conductive” as it represents an ion permeating filter. Substituting Y78 in the selectivity filter of the KcsA channel with HPLA results in an amide-to-ester substitution in the protein backbone of the selectivity filter. The carbonyl oxygen that is affected by the amide-to-ester substitution contributes to the S1 and S2 ion binding sites (
Fig. 3
A
).

We incorporated the ester substitution at Y78 in the KcsA channel by nonsense suppression using the optimized HPLA-RS plasmid and by using PLA in the growth media instead of HPLA. We observed robust expression of the Y78ester channel and the mutant channel showed a size exclusion profile that was similar to the wild type (
Fig. 3
,
B
and
C
). Using our optimized protocol, the yields of the Y78ester channel (1.4–1.88 mg/L of culture) were ∼18-fold higher than those obtained using the original approach (
Fig. 3
B
). We confirmed ester incorporation into the KcsA channel by base hydrolysis which resulted in cleavage of the ester-containing polypeptide while similar cleavage was not observed for the wild type (
Fig. 3
D
).
Next, we tested ester incorporation at Y78 in the M96V mutant of the KcsA K
+
channel. The structure of the KcsA-M96V channel shows a selectivity filter conformation that is distinct from the conductive conformation and is referred to as “constricted” (
Fig. 4
A) (
31
). In the constricted conformation, there is a disruption of the S2 and the S3 ion binding sites, which presents a barrier for ion movement through the filter (
Fig. 4
B
). The constricted conformation therefore corresponds to a non-permeating filter. In addition to the M96V channel, the constricted conformation is also observed in structures of the KcsA channel at low K
+
or when the activation gate of the channel is trapped open (
10
,
32
). We combined the Y78ester substitution with the M96V substitution to test the effect of the ester substitution on the constricted conformation.

Using our optimized approach, we observed good levels of expression for the M96V + Y78ester channel and the mutant channel showed a size exclusion profile that was similar to the wild-type channel. We sought to determine the crystal structure of the M96V + Y78ester channel to determine the effect of the ester substitution on the selectivity filter. Structures of the KcsA channel are determined in complex with a Fab. Fab complexation is used as the KcsA-Fab complex readily crystallizes and yields crystals that diffract to a higher resolution (
10
). For the M96V + Y78ester channel, we observed that complexation with the Fab caused a dissociation of the KcsA tetramer. A similar effect of tetramer dissociation on Fab binding was also observed for the KcsA-W67F and the Y82A channels (
33
). In these cases, the addition of TBA (tetra-butyl ammonium) was shown to stabilize the KcsA tetramer on Fab binding. TBA binds to the central cavity region of the channel and structural studies of the wild-type KcsA channel with TBA show that TBA binding does not perturb the structure of the channel or alter the ion occupancy at the selectivity filter sites (
34
,
35
). We tested the effect of TBA on the M96V + Y78ester mutant and observed a similar stabilization of the channel tetramer on Fab binding.
We obtained crystals of the M96V + Y78ester channel + Fab in the presence of TBA and determined the structure (
Fig. 4
C
,
Table S1
). The electron density map corresponding to the selectivity filter region is shown. The electron density at residue 78, the site of unnatural incorporation, was well resolved and clearly shows the presence of the 4′ hydroxy group on the benzyl side chain confirming the conversion of PLA to HPLA prior to incorporation (
Fig. 4
D
). Unlike the constricted filter in the M96V channel, the selectivity filter in the M96V + Y78ester channel is in the conductive state (
Fig. 4
E
).
In the wild-type KcsA selectivity filter, electron density is observed at the S1-S4 sites, which corresponds to ion binding at these sites, and roughly equal ion occupancy is observed at the S1-S4 sites (
Fig. 5
A
) (
10
,
36
). The constricted filter in the M96V channel has a distortion of the S2 and S3 sites and no ion occupancy is observed at these sites (
31
). As previously reported, the selectivity filter in the Y78ester mutant shows a lack of ion occupancy at the S2 site (
18
). Similarly, the selectivity filter in the M96V + Y78ester mutant shows a lack of ion occupancy at the S2 site (
Fig. 5
A
). Our structural studies therefore show that the incorporation of the Y78ester substitution in the M96V channel results in a stabilization of the conductive conformation and alters the ion occupancy at the S2 site in the selectivity filter.

Tyr ester substitution in the selectivity filter alters C-type inactivation
C-type inactivation is a gating process at the selectivity filter during which the filter transitions from a conductive to a non-conductive conformation thereby turning off the flux of ions through the channel (
37
). As the M96V substitution destabilizes the conductive conformation while the additional incorporation of the Y78ester substitution stabilizes the conductive conformation, we investigated the effect of these substitutions on C-type inactivation. For this purpose, we purified the M96V and the M96V + Y78ester channels, incorporated the purified channels into lipid vesicles, and used liposome patch clamping to measure channel inactivation (
12
). As controls, we also probed the wild type and the Y78ester channels.
KcsA is a pH-gated channel (
38
). With a jump in pH on the cytoplasmic side from 8.0 to 3.0, the channels rapidly activate as indicated by a rapid increase in current and then inactivate as indicated by a decay in current (
Fig. 5
B
) (
39
,
40
). In the wild-type channels, this decay in current is a relatively slow process and can be fit with a single exponential to give a time constant of ∼2 s (
Table S2
). In the M96V channel we observe a dramatic 40-fold acceleration in the inactivation properties (time constant of ∼50 msec), consistent with the destabilization of the conductive state observed in this mutant. We have previously demonstrated that the Y78ester substitution results in a channel that does not inactivate (
12
,
18
). In the M96V + Y78ester channel, we observe inactivation which takes place at a time constant of ∼1.9 s which is similar to the inactivation observed in the wild-type channel. The reduction in the inactivation rate in the M96V + Y78ester channel compared to the M96V mutant is consistent with a stabilization of the conductive conformation in the M96V + Y78ester channel compared to the M96V channel.
Using ester substitutions to probe the role of main chain H-bonds in membrane protein stability
The GlpG protein from
E. coli

41

Fig. 6
A
) (
42

43
,
44
,
45
,
46

For this purpose, we selected three Tyr residues located at distinct regions of GlpG structure for Tyr ester substitutions (

and

Discussion
Substitution of Tyr residues in proteins with HPLA results in an amide-to-ester substitution in the protein backbone. Here we design a plasmid for HPLA incorporation using amber suppression that provides higher yields of the modified proteins compared to the previously used approach. We also describe the bioconversion of PLA to HPLA in
E. coli
. The
in-situ
generation of HPLA provides an economical approach for the incorporation of Tyr esters. We use the combination of the optimized plasmid and
in situ
HPLA generation for incorporating Tyr esters into the membrane proteins, KcsA and GlpG.
The strategy of
in situ
generation of the unnatural amino acid for incorporation has previously been used for the incorporation of unnatural amino acids such as phosphothreonine, sulfotyrosine, O-methyl tyrosine, and phosphonomethyl-alanine (nhpSer) (
48
,
49
,
50
,
51
). This strategy was shown to provide higher yields of the modified proteins by increasing the intracellular availability of the unnatural amino acid. In these cases, a synthetic pathway was imported to the host cell whereas the conversion of PLA to HPLA is carried out by an endogenous host pathway. The pathway that converts PLA to HPLA in
E. coli
is presently not known but the presence of this pathway will have to be considered while generating strategies for incorporating PLA for the generation of Phe esters.
We use the facile approach to incorporate a Tyr ester in the selectivity filter of the KcsA channel with the M96V substitution. The M96V substitution destabilizes the conductive state of the selectivity filter and the filter is in the constricted state. Our structural studies show that the channel with the M96V + Y78ester substitutions shows a conductive filter and a loss of ion occupancy at the S2 site. Inactivation in the KcsA channel corresponds to a transition of the selectivity filter from the conductive state. Our functional studies show that the KcsA M96V channel shows a very fast rate of inactivation while the addition of the Y78ester substitution reduces the rate of inactivation. Our structural and functional studies therefore show that the Y78ester substitution is able to overcome the destabilization of the conductive state of the selectivity filter due to the M96V substitution.
The stabilization of the conductive state of the selectivity filter due to the ester substitution can be due to the alteration of the H-bond network surrounding the selectivity filter or due to the changes in the ion occupancy at the S2 site. A reduction in the rate of inactivation compared to the wild-type channel has been previously reported for the G77ester and the W67F channels (
12
,
33
). Crystal structures of these channels show a loss of ion occupancy at the S2 site, similar to Y78ester and the M96V + Y78ester channels (
12
,
33
). The G77ester substitution perturbs a different H-bond compared to the Y78ester substitution while there is no disruption of the H-bond network of the protein backbone in the W67F mutant. These results therefore suggest a strong link between the loss of ion occupancy at the S2 site and a relative stabilization of the conductive state of the selectivity filter. The precise mechanism underlying this effect is presently not evident but we anticipate that the facile introduction of the Y78ester substitution in the selectivity filter through the approaches described in this study will facilitate investigations to uncover this mechanism.
We used the facile approach for incorporating Tyr esters to perturb main chain H-bonds in the GlpG membrane protein for determining the contribution of these main chain H-bonds to protein stability. Using an SDS-based assay, we calculated that the disruption of the main H-bond reduces protein stability by 2 to 2.2 kcal/mol. These changes in GlpG stability with the ester substitutions measured by the SDS equilibrium unfolding/refolding assay can be validated by monitoring the kinetics of the folding and unfolding processes and by using alternate approaches for measurement of GlpG stability (
43
,
46
,
52
).
A key question in helical membrane proteins is the strength of a backbone H-bond (
53
,
54
). In the equilibrium assay used, SDS disrupts the tertiary structure of GlpG but does not affect the secondary structure (
44
). The disruption of the main chain H-bond due to the ester substitution is expected to alter the stability of the helical segments. The change in the GlpG stability measured for GlpG ester mutants using the SDS assay reflects the coupled effect of the stability of the helical segments on the tertiary structure. The changes in stability measured therefore do not directly provide the strength of the main chain H-bonds.
The contribution of the main chain H-bond to protein stability shows a dependence of on the position of the H-bond with the helical segment. The 276 amino acid long GlpG shows the presence of 10 Tyr residues that are spread throughout GlpG. Tyr ester substitutions at these sites will provide a detailed survey of the effect of perturbing the main chain H-bonds in the different parts of the structure on protein stability. The strategy can also be applied to other membrane proteins for understanding the contribution of the main chain H-bond to protein stability. The facile incorporation of Tyr esters that can be carried out using the protocol described in this study will facilitate these investigations.
Our studies on KcsA and GlpG highlight the use of the backbone ester substitutions and thereby the utility of the HPLA-RS that enables the incorporation of the ester substitution. The utility of the HPLA-RS is however limited to the incorporation of Tyr esters. We anticipate that the utility of ester substitutions will spur efforts toward the isolation of additional synthetases that can incorporate hydroxyl acids for ester substitutions across a broad range of residues.
Experimental procedures
Construction of the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid
A pBK plasmid carrying the HPLA-RS gene (
21
) and the pULTRA plasmid used (pULTRA-CNF, Addgene plasmid # 48215) were gifts from Dr Peter Schultz. Prior to the transfer of the HPLA-RS gene, the spectinomycin resistance gene on the pULTRA plasmid (
26
) was replaced by the kanamycin resistance gene from pRSF1b (EMD Millipore). This change in antibiotic resistance was necessary for carrying out protein expression in TOP10 cells. We then substituted the NotI site at the 5′ end of the pCNF-RS gene on the pULTRA plasmid with a NdeI site. We PCR amplified the HPLA-RS gene from the pBK plasmid with a 5′ NdeI and a 3′ NotI site and used this PCR fragment to exchange the pCNF-RS with the HPLA-RS gene to provide the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid (
Fig. S1
) used in this study.
Super-folder Green Fluorescent Protein (sfGFP)
Expression
SfGFP in a pBAD vector (Fisher Scientific) with a TAG stop codon at N150 and a C-terminal His tag was provided by Dr Ryan Mehl (Oregon State University) (
23
). For protein expression,
E. coli
TOP10 cells (Fisher Scientific) were transformed with the sfGFP and the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmids. The transformants were cultured in LB media at 37 °C with ampicillin (0.1 mg/ml), kanamycin (0.05 mg/ml), and 1 mM PLA (Astatech) or HPLA (ChemImpex) to an
A
600
of 1.0. Protein expression was then induced by the addition of 1 mM IPTG (for the expression of the synthetase) and 0.1 % (w/v) of arabinose (for expression of sfGFP) and the cells were grown for 4 h at 37 °C. The cells were harvested by centrifugation, and resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Hepes, pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 1 mM MgCl
2
, 0.2 mg/ml lysozyme, 0.01 mg/ml DNAse, 1 mM PMSF) and lysed by sonication. The cell lysate was clarified by centrifugation and the sfGFP proteins were purified by Co
2+
affinity chromatography. The molecular weight of the sfGFP purified was determined by Electrospray Ionization Mass spectrometry (ESI-MS) and carried out by the Proteomics Core at OHSU.
Crystallization and structure determination.
For crystallization, the C-terminal His tag was removed by treatment with trypsin in a 1:50 ratio at 4 °C for 1 h. Following trypsinolysis, the GFP proteins were purified by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) in 20 mM Hepes, pH 7.5, and 100 mM NaCl. Following purification by SEC, the GFP proteins were concentrated to 17 mg/ml, and GFP crystals were grown in sitting drops by mixing 1 μl of the protein with 1 μl of a crystallization solution (50 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 25% PEG 4000). Crystals were cryoprotected by the addition of 20% glycerol and frozen in liquid Nitrogen. X-ray diffraction data were collected at the ALS 4.2.2 beamline and the data were integrated and scaled using XDS (
55
). The structure was solved by molecular replacement using Phaser (
56
) with the wild-type SfGFP structure (PDB ID:
5EHU
) as the search model, refined using automated refinement in Phenix and manual adjustments using COOT (
57
,
58
). X-ray data collection and refinement statistics are summarized in
Table S1
.
KcsA channel
Expression
We generated a TAG stop codon at Y78 in a KcsA construct with a C-terminal His tag in a pBAD vector. We also generated KcsA constructs with an M96V and with an M96V + Y78TAG substitutions. For protein expression, KcsA-pBAD plasmids were transformed into TOP10 cells along with the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid. The transformants were cultured in LB media at 37 °C with ampicillin (0.1 mg/ml), kanamycin (0.05 mg/ml), and 1 mM PLA to an
A
600
of 1.0. Protein expression was induced by the addition of 1 mM IPTG and 0.1 % (w/v) of arabinose and the cells were grown for 4 h at 37 °C. For Y78ester incorporation into the KcsA channel using the original approach, we cloned the KcsA construct with a Y78TAG substitution into a pBAD plasmid that also contained the
Methanocaldococcus jannaschii
amber suppressor tyrosyl-tRNA gene (
21
). For protein expression, this plasmid was transformed into TOP10 cells along with a pBK plasmid bearing the HPLA-RS gene (
21
), and protein expression was carried out as previously described (
18
). The cells were harvested by centrifugation, resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 250 mM Sucrose, 1 mM MgCl
2
) and membranes were prepared as previously described (
59
). The membranes were solubilized by 2% (w/v) decyl-β-D-maltoside (DM) and the KcsA proteins were purified by Co
2+
-affinity chromatography.
Crystallization and structure determination
Prior to crystallization, the C-terminal 35 residues of the KcsA channels were removed by treatment with chymotrypsin at 1:15 ratio (chymotrypsin: protein) for 2 h at room temperature (
29
). The chymotrypsinized channels were purified by SEC in 50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM KCl, 0.25% DM, pH 7.5 (SEC buffer). The KcsA channels were complexed with a Fab fragment from KcsA IgG (
10
). The KcsA -Fab complexes were purified by SEC with 10 mM Tetra butyl ammonium iodide (TBA) added to the SEC buffer. KcsA+TBA+Fab crystals were grown by mixing 1 μl of the protein with 1 μl of well solution [25–28% PEG 400 (v/v), 50 mM magnesium acetate, 50 mM MES pH 6.0–6.5]. KcsA crystals were cryo-protected by increasing the PEG 400 concentration in the reservoir to 42% (v/v) and were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. X-ray diffraction data were collected at the ALS 4.2.2 beamline and the diffraction data were integrated and scaled using XDS (
55
).
The structures were solved by molecular replacement using Phaser (
56
) with the wild-type structure (PDB:
1K4C
) as the search model. KcsA channel residues 74 to 79, lipids, water and ions were omitted from the search model. The residues deleted from the model prior to molecular replacement were manually built using Coot (
58
). The models were refined using automated refinement in Phenix (
57
) and manual refinement using COOT. X-ray data collection and refinement statistics are summarized in the
Table S1
.
GlpG
Expression
GlpG (residues 87–276) (
60
) was PCR amplified from
E. coli
genomic DNA and cloned in a pBAD vector with a C-terminal His tag. TAG stop codons were introduced at Y160, Y205, and Y224 by Quickchange mutagenesis. For protein expression, the pBAD-GlpG- TAG plasmids were transformed into TOP10 cells along with the pULTRA-HPLA-RS plasmid. The transformants were cultured in LB media at 37 °C with 1 mM PLA. Protein expression and preparation of membranes were carried out as previously described for the KcsA channel. The membranes were solubilized by using 2% (w/v) DM and the GlpG proteins were purified by Co
2+
-affinity chromatography. The GlpG proteins were further purified by SEC in 50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM KCl, 0.25% DM, pH 7.5.
